title: My Sister Had A Habit Of Turning Every Family Dinner Into A Comedy Show About My Most Embarrassing Moments, And When She Raised Her Glass At My Engagement Dinner To Start Again, My Quiet Fiance Set Down His Drink And Told The Whole Table Th
excerpt: Every family has a storyteller. In mine, it was my older sister, Courtney.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE FAMILY COMEDIAN
Every family has a storyteller. In mine, it was my older sister, Courtney.

She was five years older than me, beautiful, quick and loud. At every holiday dinner and birthday party, Courtney held the floor. She could make our grandparents laugh until they wiped their eyes. She could make strangers at a wedding feel like old friends.

Whenever attention drifted my way, even for a moment, Courtney would lean back in her chair, smile, and say, “Oh, did I ever tell you about the time Jenna…” And then she would launch into one of a dozen stories she had polished like jewelry over the years.
There was the time I threw up on the bus during a fourth-grade field trip. The time I walked into a glass door at the mall. The time I accidentally dyed my hair green before my eighth-grade dance.
But her favorite, the one she saved for the biggest audiences, was the County Fair Story.

“When Jenna was ten,” she would begin, “Mom and Dad sent us to the county fair together, and I turned around for one second, and she was gone. Just vanished. We had half the sheriff’s department looking for her. And where do they find her? Sitting behind the cotton candy booth, bawling her eyes out, in this ridiculous yellow raincoat, with her face covered in pink sugar. A deputy had to carry her to the car. She cried the whole way home!”
I always smiled and looked down at my plate.
Because that was not what happened at the county fair. Not even close. But I had learned long ago that correcting Courtney only made the laughter louder. So for twenty years, I said nothing.
PART 2 — MEETING RYAN

I met Ryan Callahan at a hardware store, of all places, in the paint aisle. I was trying to choose between two nearly identical shades of blue for my bathroom. He was a high school science teacher buying supplies for a classroom experiment.
“That one,” he said, pointing to the darker shade. “The other one’s going to look gray under fluorescent light.”
He was right. I told him so when I ran into him again a week later at the same store, buying painter’s tape. He asked me to coffee.

Ryan was kind in a way that never needed an audience. He listened more than he talked. He remembered small things, like how I took my coffee and the name of my childhood dog. When he laughed, it was with you, never at you.
We dated for two years. He met my family at Thanksgiving the first year.
Courtney performed, of course. She told the glass door story and the green hair story. Everyone laughed. Ryan smiled politely and ate his pie.
In the car afterward, he was quiet for a long time.
“Does she always do that?” he finally asked.
I shrugged. “It’s just Courtney. She’s been doing it forever. It doesn’t bother me.”
He glanced at me. “Jenna, you went completely still every time she started a story. Like you were bracing for a blow.”
“I’m not asking you to fight with her,” he said gently. “I just want you to know that I see it. And that you never have to be the punch line with me.”

That night, I lay awake thinking about all the dinners and parties where I had sat smiling at my plate while everyone laughed. I had told myself for years that it was harmless. That it was just how my sister showed love. For the first time, I wondered whether that was true.

No one had ever noticed that before. Not my parents, not my friends, not anyone. And now that someone finally had, I realized I could never stop seeing it myself. The next holiday, I counted. Courtney told four stories about me before the turkey was even carved.
PART 3 — THE PHOTO ALBUM
Last spring, Ryan proposed on a hiking trail above a lake, with a ring that had belonged to his grandmother. I said yes before he finished the question.

A few weeks later, we visited my parents to celebrate. While Mom made lunch, she pulled out the old family photo albums to show Ryan pictures of me as a baby. Ryan sat on the couch turning pages, laughing at my school photos and my terrible eighth-grade bangs.
It was a photograph of me at ten years old, standing in front of the Ferris wheel at the Harlan County Fair, wearing a bright yellow raincoat with a hood shaped like a duck’s bill.
“Jenna,” he said slowly. “What year was this?”
He didn’t answer. He took out his phone, snapped a picture of the photo, and texted it to someone. Then he closed the album and smiled at my mother as if nothing had happened.
That night, I asked him what that was about.
“I’m not sure yet,” he said. “I need to check something with my mom.”
His mother, Patricia, lived two hours away. I had met her only twice. She was a retired nurse, warm and gentle, with the same quiet way of listening as her son.

Two days later, Ryan came home from school, set down his bag, and looked at me with an expression I had never seen on his face before. “Jenna,” he said, “I think I’ve known about you since I was eight years old.”
PART 4 — THE OTHER STORY
He sat me down on our couch and told me a story I had never heard. His family’s version of the Harlan County Fair, 2004.

Ryan’s little brother, Danny, was three years old that summer. Their mother, Patricia, had taken both boys to the fair. In the crowd near the livestock barn, Danny let go of her hand. In thirty seconds, he was gone.

“My mom says it was the worst hour of her life,” Ryan told me. “She ran through that whole fair screaming his name. I was eight, holding her hand, crying. The sheriff’s deputies were searching everywhere. They were talking about closing the gates.”
They finally found Danny behind the cotton candy booth, near the far parking lot. He was sitting on an overturned bucket, wrapped in a yellow raincoat much too big for him, eating cotton candy.
And beside him, holding his hand, was a little girl about ten years old, shivering in a T-shirt.

“She had found him wandering near the parking lot, right by the road where the trucks were coming in,” Ryan said. “He was crying. She picked him up, carried him away from the traffic, put her own raincoat on him because it had started to drizzle, and gave him her cotton candy to calm him down. She wouldn’t leave him. A teenage worker tried to take Danny to the office, and she refused. She said she promised she’d stay until his mom came.”

“My mom has told that story at every family gathering for twenty years,” he said. “The brave little girl in the yellow duck raincoat who saved Danny. She never got her name. The girl ran off before my mom could thank her properly. The deputy had to carry her back to her family because her sister had left her alone.”
He took my hand. “I texted my mom the photo,” he said. “She cried for an hour. Jenna, it was you. It was always you.”
PART 5 — THE TRUTH I NEVER TOLD
Because Ryan was right. I remembered every second of that day, though I had never told anyone the whole truth.

Courtney was fifteen. Mom and Dad sent us to the fair together and told her to keep an eye on me. Within twenty minutes, she met a boy named Kyle from the high school football team. She handed me five dollars, told me to buy cotton candy and wait by the Ferris wheel, and disappeared with him.
I waited for an hour. She never came back.

I wandered toward the parking lot looking for her. That was where I found a tiny boy in a striped shirt, crying, walking straight toward the road where the livestock trucks were pulling in. I grabbed him just as a big truck turned the corner.
I didn’t know what else to do. So I sat with him behind the cotton candy booth, wrapped him in my raincoat, shared my cotton candy, and sang him every song I knew until a deputy found us.
When his mother came running, I was so relieved I started crying. Then I panicked, because I realized I was going to be in huge trouble for leaving the Ferris wheel. So I ran.
The deputy caught up with me and drove me to the main gate, where Courtney was waiting, furious and scared. She made me promise not to tell Mom and Dad that she had left me.
“If you tell,” she said, “I’ll get grounded all summer, and it’ll be your fault.”
So when we got home, she told our parents her version. That I had wandered off. That I got lost. That I cried. That a deputy had to bring me home.
And I was ten years old and loved my big sister, so I let her tell it. And then I let her tell it again, and again, every holiday for twenty years.
PART 6 — THE ENGAGEMENT DINNER

Our engagement dinner was held at an Italian restaurant in town. Both families were there. My parents, my grandmother, Courtney and her husband, a few aunts and uncles. On Ryan’s side, his father, his mother Patricia, and his younger brother Danny, now twenty-three and studying to be a paramedic.
Patricia hugged me so hard at the door that I could barely breathe. She did not say anything. She just held my face in her hands and looked at me with tears in her eyes.
Ryan had asked her not to say anything yet. He had a plan.

Dinner was lovely. The pasta was wonderful. My father gave a sweet toast. Ryan’s father told funny stories about Ryan as a boy. And then, just as dessert arrived, Courtney tapped her wine glass with a spoon and stood up.
